prompt:

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?

   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?

   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?

   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?

   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?

   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: WD co-leads hard drives, a mature industry now riding AI data growth, and the stock rose about 176% over 52 weeks, but it is not a top dog in an emerging industry, its brand is not a household default, and it lacks a famous anchor investor. It fits only some Rule Breaker traits, mainly momentum and the AI data trend.
summaries.buffett: The business is simple and sits in a rational three-player industry with strong current cash flow ($3.5B FY2026 free cash flow) and a clean balance sheet, but results have been cyclical, with operating losses in FY2023-FY2024 and no dividend from 2020 until 2025. At about 32x non-GAAP trailing earnings and 13.5x book, there is no clear margin of safety by Buffett's standards.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the three-player industry structure and the decades of hard-to-copy recording know-how, but would note the dependence on a few cloud customers (top 10 were 73% of FY2026 revenue), the cloud capex cycle and flash substitution as ways it could disappoint. It is a decent business at a cyclical peak rather than a wonderful one at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: WD is a classic cyclical in an AI-driven upcycle: revenue rose 36% in FY2026 and consensus expects non-GAAP EPS to roughly double to about $20.53 in FY2027, giving a forward P/E of about 16 and a PEG well below 1. Lynch would caution that cyclicals look cheapest on peak earnings, insiders are selling and the share count rose about 6.7% year on year.
summaries.fisher: WD keeps investing in new technology (R&D of $1,161M in FY2026) and has a clear roadmap from 40TB UltraSMR drives to 44TB HAMR in 2027 and 100TB by 2029, plus high-bandwidth and dual-pivot drives, which fits Fisher's focus on product pipelines. Its sales skill reflects tight industry supply more than unusual salesmanship, and margins have only recently become high.
summaries.graham: WD fails most of Graham's defensive tests: it lost money in FY2023 and FY2024, paid no dividend from 2020 to 2025, and trades at about 13.7x inflated GAAP earnings and 13.5x book (P/E x P/B near 185). It is large and now financially strong, but not a Graham-style bargain.
summaries.thiel: WD is one of only three hard drive makers, a durable oligopoly with direct channels to every major cloud provider and good timing with AI data growth. But it has no tenfold technology lead (Seagate's HAMR drives are ahead), it did not start by dominating a small niche, and it is not founder-led, so it answers only some of Thiel's questions well.
summaries.gerstner: WD benefits directly from AI infrastructure spending, with 89% of FY2026 revenue from cloud, fast growth, high margins and a forward P/E around 16. Gerstner would weigh that against hardware cyclicality, the stock's roughly 54% fall from its June 2026 high and the risk that HDD pricing has peaked.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating (Q1 FY2027 guidance of about $4.00 non-GAAP EPS versus $3.56 in Q4 FY2026) and the AI data cycle is a clear driver, which suits Druckenmiller's focus on earnings momentum. However, the sharp drawdown since June on HDD supply and pricing worries, target cuts from UBS and Wells Fargo in October 2026, and a high beta (about 2.2) suggest the market is debating how long the cycle lasts.
summaries.smith: WD now has high gross margins (48.9% in FY2026), strong free cash flow and low debt, but Terry Smith prefers companies with consistently high returns through the cycle, and WD's hard drive business lost money in FY2023-FY2024. Its dependence on a few cloud customers and the hardware cycle make it a poor fit for buy-and-hold-forever investing.
summaries.greenblatt: On trailing numbers WD has a high return on capital (ROIC about 53%), but its earnings yield is modest at an EV/EBIT of about 27, so operating profit is only about 3.7% of enterprise value. It would not rank near the top of a Magic Formula screen today.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool asks for a great business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high returns; WD has strong current returns and capable operators but a cyclical history and limited reinvestment needs (capex about 3% of revenue), so most cash goes to buybacks and dividends. It fits partially at best.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for low-risk, high-uncertainty bets bought cheaply in simple businesses; WD is simple and now has net cash, but the industry is in an upcycle rather than a temporary setback, and the stock at about 26x free cash flow is not priced for heads-I-win outcomes. Downside could be large if HDD pricing turns.
summaries.wood: WD supplies storage for AI data, but it is a 1970-founded hard drive maker rather than a disruptive innovator in ARK's platforms, and hard drives face long-term substitution by flash. Its falling cost per terabyte (about 10% a year expected) helps, but its market is not set to grow many times over in five years.
summaries.ackman: WD is simple and cash-generative with low debt after retiring most of its convertible notes, but it is not a predictable, dominant business with pricing power insulated from the economy; results depend heavily on cloud capex and HDD pricing. It fits Ackman's criteria only partly.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured companies that share scale savings with customers to grow ever stronger; WD is instead raising price per terabyte (up by a 'high teens' rate year on year in Q4 FY2026) in a tight market. Its position in 10-20 years is uncertain given flash substitution and Toshiba's expansion.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products solving painful problems, timed with technology shifts; WD solves the large problem of storing the world's data cheaply and is well timed to AI data growth. But it is a mature incumbent rather than a young company creating a new market.
summaries.nash: WD sells infrastructure for AI and cloud data with strong numbers (revenue growth 36%, operating margin 34.5%, cash above debt, consistent earnings beats) and scores about 95 on Nash's 13 categories. It falls short on Nash's DCF at a 12% discount rate, on insider selling, on a CEO in the job less than two years, and on its five-year record, which includes a revenue drop and losses in FY2023.

momentum.evidence: WDC is up about 176% over 52 weeks to $332.00 (Oct 16, 2026 close), far ahead of the market, but it has fallen about 54% from its mid-June 2026 intraday high near $717.

g4.evidence: CEO Irving Tan (ex-Cisco COO) has delivered record results since 2025 and institutions own about 88% of shares, but no famous anchor investor or partner is publicly associated with the stock.

g6.evidence: Fox Advisors downgraded it in June 2026 saying HDD pricing expectations ran ahead of reality and UBS rates it Hold, but the consensus is Buy with an average target of $668.50, about double the price.

simple.evidence: WD makes and sells hard drives, 89% of them to cloud data centers, a business a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Results swing with the cycle: continuing-operations revenue fell from $9,039M in FY2022 to $6,255M in FY2023 with operating losses in FY2023 and FY2024, then rose to a record $12,919M in FY2026.

integrity.evidence: Management cut debt from $4.7B to $1.05B in FY2026, reinstated a dividend and bought back $2.6B of stock, but the share count still rose about 6.7% year on year after convertible-note settlements and insiders, including the CEO, have been net sellers.

b6.evidence: WD split off its flash business as Sandisk in February 2025 to focus on hard drives and says it is not adding drive-unit capacity, rather than building an empire.

roic.evidence: Trailing ROIC is about 53% with little debt, but the hard drive business made operating losses in FY2023 ($548M) and FY2024 ($403M), so returns have not been consistent.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $3,511M (operating cash flow $3,929M less $418M capex), about 89% of non-GAAP net income of $3,943M (GAAP net income of $9,424M includes a $6.5B Sandisk gain).

b10.evidence: WD's market value has risen to about $124B as operating income went from $409M (FY2022) to $4,453M (FY2026), but much of that reflects an industry upcycle rather than steadily compounding retained earnings.

safety.evidence: At $332 the stock trades at about 32x non-GAAP trailing earnings, 13.5x book and a 2.8% free-cash-flow yield, so there is no margin of safety against a conservative value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 16 and PEG of about 0.2 look reasonable if FY2027 consensus non-GAAP EPS of $20.53 is met, but those are peak-cycle earnings.

mu5.evidence: It could be hurt by an AI/cloud capex pause, Toshiba's planned capacity doubling, Seagate's HAMR lead, flash substitution or customer concentration (three customers were 16%, 15% and 13% of FY2026 revenue).

reinvest.evidence: It needs little capital (FY2026 capex $418M, about 3% of revenue) and reinvests mainly through $1,161M of R&D, while most cash goes to buybacks ($2,592M) and debt reduction.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical: an AI-driven upcycle in nearline storage after operating losses in FY2023-FY2024.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 16 is far below expected EPS growth (consensus FY2027 non-GAAP EPS $20.53 vs $10.22 in FY2026, about 101%), a PEG of about 0.2.

runway.evidence: The CFO expects exabyte growth above 25% a year over the next 3-5 years and customers are discussing agreements to 2031, but revenue growth depends on pricing and the cycle.

ly7.evidence: Aggregated Form 4 data show no open-market insider purchases and about 110 sales in the six months to October 2026 (CEO Tan sold about 40,000 shares), and the share count rose about 6.7% year on year.

ly8.evidence: It is widely covered (26 analysts), joined the Nasdaq-100, and was a high-profile AI storage trade in 2025-2026.

fi2.evidence: WD began volume production of 40TB UltraSMR ePMR drives in the June 2026 quarter and plans 44TB HAMR drives in 1H 2027, 50TB in 2H 2027 and 100TB by 2029.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $1,161M in FY2026 produced the 40TB ePMR drive, UltraSMR (expected to reach about 60% of nearline exabytes by end-FY2027) and high-bandwidth drives sampling with five customers, as gross margin rose to 48.9%.

fi4.evidence: It sells effectively to hyperscalers through long-term agreements (one through calendar 2029), but this reflects industry supply tightness more than unusual sales skill.

longterm.evidence: WD funds long-range projects (HAMR, dual-pivot drives for 2028, a software platform for 2027) but trails Seagate in HAMR and directs most cash to buybacks and dividends.

gr1.evidence: Revenue was $12.9B in FY2026 and the market value is about $124B.

ni10.evidence: WD reported net losses in FY2023 and FY2024 (continuing operations lost $902M and $765M).

gr4.evidence: WD suspended its dividend in 2020 and its board adopted a new quarterly dividend program only in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS rose from $1.06 in FY2016 to $24.28 in FY2026 (FY2026 includes a $6.5B Sandisk gain; non-GAAP EPS was $10.22).

gr6.evidence: With losses in FY2023-FY2024 the average earnings are low, and the price is about 32x trailing non-GAAP EPS, far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 13.7 (inflated by the Sandisk gain) times a P/B of about 13.5 is about 185, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its 40TB ePMR drive leads conventional recording, but there is no tenfold advantage, and Seagate's HAMR drives already reach 44TB.

timing.evidence: AI data growth and tight HDD supply let WD raise prices as exabyte shipments grew 26% year on year in the June 2026 quarter, with 40TB drives just entering volume production.

th3.evidence: WD has been a large player in a large hard drive market for decades rather than starting from a dominant share of a small niche.

team.evidence: Management is experienced and executing well (record FY2026 results), but it is a professional team led by a CEO in the role since 2025, not a founder-led or widely celebrated one.

th5.evidence: It sells directly to every major cloud provider (top 10 customers were 73% of FY2026 revenue) and through OEM, distributor and retail channels worldwide.

durable.evidence: The three-player structure and recording know-how should hold for years, but cheaper flash memory could shrink the hard drive market over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its bet on stretching conventional ePMR with UltraSMR to 40TB while preparing HAMR is a differentiated path, but rivals see the same AI storage opportunity.

dr2.evidence: The 40TB ePMR and 44TB HAMR ramps and long-term contracts should help, but Toshiba's capacity doubling by fiscal 2027 could weigh on pricing within that window.

dr4.evidence: Strong AI data center spending helps, but the business is economically sensitive (beta about 2.2), though it now has more cash ($1,579M) than debt ($1,052M).

dr6.evidence: Q1 FY2027 results on Oct 22, 2026 (guidance $4.1B revenue, about $4.00 EPS), the 44TB HAMR launch in 1H 2027 and new long-term agreements are near-term catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Earnings momentum is strong, but cyclicality and the roughly 54% drop from the June 2026 high argue against a very large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin reached 48.9% in FY2026 and 54.4% (non-GAAP) in the June 2026 quarter, high for hardware but up from 22.2% in FY2023.

fcfyield.evidence: The trailing free-cash-flow yield is about 2.8% ($3.5B on a $124B market value), thin for a cyclical hardware company even with fast growth.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 27, so operating profit is only about 3.7% of enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: The business is in an upcycle with record results; the stock's drop since June reflects worries about future HDD pricing, not a current setback.

pa4.evidence: The business is strongly cash-generative with net cash and three-player economics, but at peak-cycle earnings a downturn could cause large, lasting losses for buyers at today's price.

wo1.evidence: It is a leading supplier of storage for AI data but not an AI technology leader itself.

wo2.evidence: WD expects cost per terabyte to fall about 10% a year, but it is currently raising price per terabyte rather than passing savings on.

wo3.evidence: It is focused on one platform, magnetic hard drive storage, since spinning off flash.

wo4.evidence: Management expects exabyte growth above 25% a year, which is strong but not a market many times larger in five years.

ns1.evidence: WD is raising price per terabyte (up by a 'high teens' rate year on year in Q4 FY2026) rather than sharing scale savings with customers.
